plain_english: I'm amazed when I see people asking others for their time, and how willingly they give it. Both sides think about what the time will be used for, but neither thinks about the time itself. It's as if asking for time costs nothing and giving it away is free. We waste the most precious thing we have. People don't notice this because time isn't something you can touch or see. So we treat it as worthless — or nearly worthless. People treasure gifts and money. They work hard for wages and benefits. But no one values time. They give it away freely, as if it costs nothing.
original_excerpt: I am filled with wonder when I see some men asking others for their time, and those who are asked for it most willing to give it: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself, as though in asking for this one asked for nothing, and in giving it one gave nothing: we play with what is the most precious of all things: yet it escapes men's notice, because it is an incorporeal thing, and because it does not come before our eyes; and therefore it is held very cheap, nay, hardly any value whatever is put upon it. Men set the greatest store upon presents or pensions, and hire out their work, their services, or their care in order to gain them: no one values time: they give it much more freely, as though it cost nothing.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8

plain_english: Yet you'll see these same people begging their doctor on their knees when they're sick and facing death. If charged with a crime that could kill them, they'd give away everything they own just to stay alive. How contradictory they are! If we could see exactly how many years each person had left — the way we can count the years already behind us — how desperately those with only a few years remaining would try to use them well. It's easy to manage any amount carefully when you know exactly how much you have. But the thing you should guard most carefully is something that might run out at any moment — and you never know when.
original_excerpt: Yet you will see these same people clasping the knees of their physician as suppliants when they are sick and in present peril of death, and if threatened with a capital charge willing to give all that they possess in order that they may live: so inconsistent are they. Indeed, if the number of every man's future years could be laid before him, as we can lay that of his past years, how anxious those who found that they had but few years remaining would be to make the most of them? Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8

plain_english: You might think people don't understand how precious time is. But they do know. When they love someone deeply, they say they'd give up years of their own life for them. And they actually do give up those years — they just don't realize they're doing it. They give away their time in ways that cost them everything but give the other person nothing. The problem is they don't know where their time comes from, so they can stand to waste what they can't see. But here's the truth: no one will ever give you back those lost years. No one can restore them. Once your life starts moving, it won't stop or start over. It won't undo what's already been done.
original_excerpt: Yet you have no reason to suppose that they do not know how dear a thing time is: they are wont to say to those whom they especially love that they are ready to give them a part of their own years. They do give them, and know not that they are giving them; but they give them in such a manner that they themselves lose them without the others gaining them. They do not, however, know whence they obtain their supply, and therefore they are able to endure the waste of what is not seen: yet no one will give you back your years, no one will restore them to you again: your life will run its course when once it has begun, and will neither begin again or efface what it has done.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8

plain_english: Time won't make a sound as it passes. It won't warn you how fast it's flying by. It moves in complete silence. No king can order it to slow down. No nation can wish it away. Time runs the same steady pace from your first day to your last. It never turns aside. It never delays. So what does this mean? You're busy with your life, but life is racing past you. Death will arrive someday, and when he does, you'll have to pay attention — whether you want to or not.
original_excerpt: It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on: it will not prolong itself at the command of a king, or at the wish of a nation: as it started on its first day, so it will run: it will never turn aside, never delay. What follows, then? Why! you are busy, but life is hurrying on: death will be here some time or other, and you must attend to him, whether you will or no.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8
